meta.subtitle: AI datacenter power-delivery specialist; strong Q2 execution and rising royalties against a rich multiple

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Vicor a BUY with a 12-month target range of $300 to $420 against a price of $268.34. Vicor designs and manufactures modular power components and systems, and its Advanced Products line has become a supplier of high-density power delivery for AI and datacenter processors. Second-quarter results showed the ramp taking hold: revenue rose sharply year over year, backlog expanded to more than double its year-ago level, and gross and operating margins recovered from a weak FY24. The balance sheet is unusually clean, with a large cash position and no funded debt, which lets the company fund a planned capacity expansion from internal resources. The counter-case is price. After rising from a 52-week low of $47.56, the shares carry a premium multiple that already discounts years of the growth consensus models. Our Base case sits below the consensus target, and our Bear case implies a decline of more than a quarter, reflecting the compression that would follow any stumble in a customer-concentrated, historically cyclical business. On our probability weighting the balance still favors owning the shares, but this is a BUY held with clear sight of the valuation.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Vicor Corporation designs, develops, manufactures, and markets modular power components and power systems that convert electrical power for electrically powered devices. The company was incorporated in 1981 and is headquartered in Andover, Massachusetts. Management groups the portfolio into Advanced Products, which implement its proprietary Factorized Power Architecture and are used for power delivery on server motherboards, in server racks, and across datacenter infrastructure, and Brick Products, its established families of integrated converters sold into aerospace and defense, industrial, instrumentation, and transportation markets. Vicor states it has established a leadership position in the emerging market segment for powering high-performance processors used for the acceleration of artificial intelligence applications. Its AI customers include leading processor and accelerator designers alongside early adopters in cloud and high-performance computing. The company reports revenue as a single consolidated total and does not break out sales by product line or geography in its statements. For FY25, revenue was $407.7 million, up 13.5%, with net income of $118.6 million and diluted EPS of $2.61.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: Vicor is executing a deliberate shift from many small customers toward a smaller number of large OEM and ODM accounts, concentrated in the datacenter and hyperscaler segments where its parts power AI processors. The evidence that the shift is working sits in the order book, the product mix, and the margin trend, all of which the sections below quantify: backlog and Advanced Products revenue are growing rapidly, and gross and operating margins are recovering from a weak FY24. Management also intends to expand intellectual-property licensing, which would add a high-margin, capacity-light revenue stream. The tension in the stock is not the business but the price: the shares carry a premium multiple that already discounts years of the growth consensus models. Our BUY rests on continued conversion of the backlog and disciplined execution on capacity, tempered by a Bear case that de-rates the shares hard if concentrated demand slips.

catalysts: Conversion of a sharply larger order book into revenue as AI and datacenter demand absorbs fab capacity.
A planned second fab that would relieve the capacity constraint now limiting shipments.
Continued growth in intellectual-property licensing, a higher-margin revenue stream management intends to expand.
Further gross-margin recovery as volume and product mix improve off the current quarterly run-rate.
risks: Valuation: the shares carry a premium multiple that leaves little room for disappointment.
Customer concentration: a few large customers can disproportionately move quarterly results.
Trade exposure: roughly half of revenue is earned abroad, exposing results to tariffs and trade policy.
Comparability: prior-year results were distorted by a one-time litigation settlement, and royalty income is lumpy.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter 2026 total net revenues were $143.4 million, a 26.9% sequential increase from $113.0 million in the first quarter and a 49.3% increase from the prior-year quarter. Reported gross margin was 58.0% of net revenues, up from 55.2% in the first quarter. A year earlier the gross-margin line was 65.3%, but that figure included a $45.0 million patent litigation settlement recognized in the second quarter of 2025; the same settlement lifted the full-year FY25 gross margin to 63.6%, so neither is a clean, product-based run-rate. Operating expenses rose to $48.2 million from $45.5 million, as higher selling, general and administrative expense outweighed lower research and development expense, and income from operations produced a second-quarter operating margin of 24.3%. Net income was $49.8 million, or $1.04 per diluted share, up from $20.7 million, or $0.44 per diluted share, in the first quarter and $41.2 million, or $0.91 per diluted share, a year ago. Management noted that both 2026 quarters carried tax benefits from excess deductions related to share-based compensation. FY25 produced a 20.1% operating margin, a sharp recovery from FY24, when the operating margin was -0.4% and diluted EPS was $0.14. On a trailing-twelve-month basis the operating margin is 18.6% and the net margin is 30.6%; the net margin sits above the operating margin because of the 2026 share-based-compensation tax benefits and other income, both of which fall inside the trailing window, and not because of the 2025 settlement, which does not.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Vicor ended the second quarter with cash and equivalents of $453.6 million, a 12.2% sequential increase from $404.2 million. The company carries no funded debt, and its trailing-twelve-month current ratio is 13.25, an unusually liquid position. The prior accrued-litigation balance was paid down during the period, removing a liability the company had carried into 2026. Inventories rose about 10.2% sequentially, which management attributes to building ahead of scheduled backlog rather than to softening demand. Taken together, the balance sheet lets the company fund its planned capacity expansion from internal resources without raising external capital.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow was $34.0 million in the second quarter, a swing from the $3.9 million used in operations in the first quarter, which had absorbed a $28.6 million payment of a past litigation award. A year earlier, operating cash flow was $65.2 million. Capital expenditures were $11.2 million in the quarter, versus $12.4 million in the first quarter and $6.2 million a year ago, as the company invests in manufacturing capacity. For the full year FY25, free cash flow was $119.2 million on an FCF margin of 29.2%, and the company repurchased $35.2 million of stock, a modest sum relative to that cash generation. The trailing free-cash-flow yield is only 0.4%, a direct consequence of the current valuation rather than of weak cash generation.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Vicor trades at 86.0x trailing earnings and 26.1x sales, multiples that only make sense against the growth the company is now posting. On forward estimates the multiple compresses: the shares are at 71.9x the next twelve months of earnings and about 47.7x FY27E EPS of $5.62, with FY26E EPS of $3.73 as the bridge between the two. A trailing EV/EBITDA figure is not carried in the pack, so we do not quote one. The FactPack also includes no peer multiples, so we anchor valuation on the company's own history and on the Street rather than on a peer group. Four analysts cover the stock, all rating it Buy, with a consensus price target of $386.25, a median of $387.50, and a range of $320.00 to $450.00. Our own target range is more conservative than the consensus midpoint, reflecting the downside embedded in a high multiple.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: AI and datacenter demand keeps Advanced Products and the backlog compounding, the planned second fab adds capacity on schedule, and licensing revenue scales; earnings grow into a still-premium multiple.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Backlog converts steadily and margins hold near current levels, but growth decelerates from the second quarter's pace and the multiple drifts lower as the AI-capacity build matures.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A few large customers pull in or cancel orders, or AI power-delivery competition intensifies; revenue growth stalls and the premium multiple compresses toward the broad market, driving a fresh de-rating well below recent levels.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bull at 30%, and the Bear at 25%. The Base case implies $360, below the consensus target but above today's price. The Bull case implies $450 on continued AI-driven compounding of revenue and licensing income. The Bear case implies $190, and it anchors the risk in this name: a customer-concentrated business trading at a high multiple has a long way to fall if growth disappoints. The probability-weighted outcome supports a BUY rather than a stronger rating, because the expected reward and the downside are close to balanced.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Vicor reports as a single reportable segment, shown as one consolidated total rather than a product or geographic split. Within that business, management runs two product categories. Advanced Products implement the Factorized Power Architecture and serve large OEMs, ODMs, and their contract manufacturers, with sales concentrated in data center and hyperscaler computing and in powering AI processors; this line is growing far faster than the rest of the company, as the growth section quantifies. Brick Products are the established integrated converters sold to a fragmented base in aerospace and defense, industrial equipment, instrumentation, and transportation; this line grew 2.4% sequentially in the second quarter. The company does not disclose revenue by category or region in its statements, though it notes export sales were roughly 46.0% of second-quarter net revenues. The strategy is a deliberate shift toward fewer, higher-volume customers, which raises both the growth potential and the concentration risk.

moatFactors.name: Proprietary power-conversion IP
moatFactors.body: Vicor's products rely on patented high-frequency switching topologies and its Factorized Power Architecture, implemented in proprietary semiconductor circuitry, materials, and packaging. The company earns royalty revenue by licensing this intellectual property and states it intends to expand that licensing, evidence that the IP has standalone value competitors cannot easily replicate.

moatFactors.name: AI power-delivery position
moatFactors.body: Vicor states it has established a leadership position in the emerging segment for powering high-performance AI processors, with customers among leading processor and accelerator designers. Its second-generation VPD roadmap targets the current-density and power-delivery-network limits that constrain GPUs, TPUs, and wafer-scale engines.

moatFactors.name: Manufacturing integration
moatFactors.body: Vicor produces advanced parts in its own ChiP fab and has moved outsourced package steps in-house to manage supply risk. Control of manufacturing supports differentiation, but it also ties margins to factory utilization, which cuts both ways across the cycle.

moatFactors.name: Design-in switching costs
moatFactors.body: Power-conversion parts are designed into customer platforms, which creates switching costs once a design win is secured. The same concentration means the loss of a single large program would be felt disproportionately.

businessMoat.durability: The durability of Vicor's advantage is real but bounded. On the positive side, the IP and licensing model, the AI power-delivery position, and the investment in a second fab point to an edge that can persist for several years. On the other side, the business is small, historically cyclical, and increasingly concentrated in a few large customers whose order timing can swing results sharply; the company itself lists customer concentration, supply-chain reliance on outsourced package steps, and competitive price actions among its risks. Competition in AI power delivery is intensifying as alternative approaches such as point-of-load regulators and integrated voltage regulators evolve. On balance the moat is genuine but narrow: strong enough to earn premium margins in good periods, not wide enough to insulate the company from the electronics cycle or from a major customer's decision.

points: AI and datacenter power delivery is the main growth engine. Advanced Products revenue grew 45.0% sequentially in the second quarter, and twelve-month backlog reached about $380 million, up 145% from a year ago. The mechanism is design wins for on-board and in-rack power delivery converting into repeatable, high-volume orders; what to watch is whether that backlog ships on schedule.

Intellectual-property licensing is a distinct, higher-margin revenue stream. As Vicor licenses its power-conversion patents to third parties, royalty income scales with customers' unit volumes rather than with Vicor's own factory output, so incremental royalties carry very high margins. The risk is that royalty timing is lumpy and depends on negotiated agreements.

Capacity is the binding near-term constraint. Management says its existing fab is nearing full utilization and it is taking steps toward a second fab for high current-density second-generation VPD parts; until that capacity arrives, revenue growth is limited by what the current line can build. What to watch is the timeline and cost of the second fab.

Consensus models a steep ramp, with FY26E revenue of about $622.3 million, up 53%, and FY27E revenue of $945.4 million. Those estimates assume both continued AI demand and the capacity to serve it; execution against the backlog is what would validate them.

Gross margin is recovering on volume and mix, and the second-quarter run-rate already sits above the trailing-twelve-month average of 56.6%. The organic target is that run-rate rather than the FY25 headline gross margin, which the financials section shows was inflated by a one-time litigation settlement and is not a clean baseline.

management.leadership: Vicor is led by Dr. Patrizio Vinciarelli, President and Chief Executive Officer, with James F. Schmidt as Chief Financial Officer. For 2025 the named executive officers were the President and CEO, the CFO, and three Corporate Vice Presidents. The proxy describes a centralized process in which the CEO makes periodic compensation recommendations to the Compensation Committee for the other executives. Leadership has overseen a sharp recovery in profitability over the past year while establishing the company's position in AI power delivery.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation prioritizes reinvestment over shareholder returns. Vicor pays no dividend and is directing cash into manufacturing capacity, including the planned second fab. The buybacks and free cash flow detailed in the cash-flow section were modest relative to that cash generation, so the company is retaining capital to fund growth rather than returning it. With no debt and a large cash balance, it can self-fund the expansion. The open question is the return on that capacity investment, which depends on sustained high-volume demand from a small number of customers.
management.governance: Governance rests on the proxy statement filed April 30, 2026. Vicor holds its say-on-pay advisory vote every three years, most recently in 2023, when shareholders approved the executive compensation program. Compensation combines base salary, contingent cash bonuses concentrated in sales and marketing roles, stock options, and an employee stock purchase plan; executives are employees at will without employment contracts. One related-party arrangement stands out: a director and nominee, Andrew T. D'Amico, also serves as the company's general counsel for intellectual-property matters, receiving a monthly fee plus an incentive fee equal to 3% of royalties on certain license agreements he negotiates, capped at $1,000,000. Because that arrangement ties a director's pay to the same licensing revenue the company is expanding, it deserves ongoing scrutiny.
management.insiderOwnership: The captured proxy excerpt does not include beneficial-ownership tables, so we cannot quantify insider or institutional holdings from the pack. The related-party general-counsel arrangement noted above is the principal insider economic interest disclosed in the excerpt.

idiosyncratic: Customer concentration: the strategic focus on a few large OEM, ODM, and contract-manufacturing customers means unanticipated order delays or cancellations from a relative few can disproportionately lower revenue, as the company states in its risk factors.
Valuation risk: the premium multiple discussed in the valuation section prices in sustained rapid growth, so any deceleration could compress it sharply.

Cyclicality and margin volatility: results swing with the electronics cycle, and as recently as FY24 the company posted an operating loss; quarterly gross margin varies with volume, mix, licensing income, and tariffs.

Comparability and lumpiness: as the financials section details, prior-period results were distorted by a one-time patent litigation settlement, and royalty income is uneven, so headline growth and margin comparisons can mislead.
Trade and tariff exposure: Section 301 tariffs equaled about 1.8% of net revenues in 2025 and rose 76.1% year over year, and China and Hong Kong accounted for roughly 11.9% of 2025 revenue.
risks.systemic: Vicor is exposed to broad forces outside its control. Roughly half of revenue is earned outside the United States, at 50.8% in 2025, so trade policy, tariffs, export controls, and the strength of the U.S. dollar all bear on demand and margins. The company sells into the electronics supply chain, which is cyclical and subject to inventory corrections. Its growth is increasingly tied to AI and datacenter capital spending, so a slowdown in that investment cycle would hit orders directly. Finally, macroeconomic weakness or defense-budget pressure would weigh on the industrial, aerospace, and defense demand that anchors the Brick Products line.

body: We rate Vicor a BUY with a target range of $300 to $420. The case is straightforward: the company has a differentiated, IP-backed position in power delivery for AI and datacenter systems, and the order book and quarterly results show that position converting into rapid growth and recovering margins. A debt-free balance sheet with a large cash position funds the capacity expansion that should sustain the ramp.

The rating is a BUY rather than a stronger call because valuation already reflects much of the opportunity, and the business carries real, identifiable downside from customer concentration and cyclicality. Our Bear case implies $190, and the probability-weighted outcome leaves reward and risk close to balanced. We would grow more constructive on evidence that royalty licensing and the second fab are scaling on schedule, and more cautious on any sign that a large customer's demand is slipping.
